"After that, we put up a wire fence."

"A wire fence?"

"Yes. You suggested it yourself some two or three years back."

"Oh, I recollect—the first time the Church tested her power against us, and soon decided she had better await a more promising opportunity. Well, how have you set the fence out?"

"I lead twelve enormously stout wires—bare, without insulation—from a large dynamo inside the cave, with only two brushes, one positive and one negative—"

"Yes, quite right."

"They run out of the cave to enclose a level circle a hundred yards across. There are twelve separate fences, spaced ten feet apart—twelve rings, one inside another—and the ends lead back into the cave."

"Right; continue."

"The fences are secured to stout oak posts, set only three feet apart and buried five feet deep."

"That should be thoroughly strong."

"Yes. None of the wires is connected to earth outside the cave. They leave the positive brush; the negative brush has an earth connection; and their returning ends are each separately grounded inside the cave."

"No, no, that won't answer!"

"Why not?"

"It costs too much—squanders power needlessly. You need no connection to earth besides the negative brush. Bring each wire's other end back into the cave and fasten it separately, without grounding it. Now see how economical that is. A cavalry force charges the fence. Until the horses strike the wire, you consume no power and spend nothing, because there is only one earth connection. At the instant they touch it, they connect themselves to the negative brush through the earth, and fall dead. Do you understand? No energy is consumed until required. Your lightning waits ready, like a charge in a gun, and costs you nothing until you fire it. Yes, a single connection to earth—"

"Of course! How did I miss that? Besides being cheaper, it's more effective, since broken or tangled wires can do no damage."

"None, particularly with an indicator in the cave to let us disconnect a broken wire. Well, what next? The gatlings?"

"Yes, those are ready. At the middle of the innermost ring, on a broad platform six feet tall, I've stationed thirteen gatling guns together and laid in plenty of ammunition."

"Exactly. They cover every avenue of approach, and there'll be music when the Church's knights appear. As for the cliff's edge above the cave—"

"There's a wire fence up there, and a gatling.

This brief understanding with Mr. Knightley afforded Emma a great deal of pleasure. It numbered among the delightful memories of the ball that she took out upon the lawn to enjoy the following morning. She was exceedingly pleased that they had reached such agreement about the Eltons, and that their judgments of husband and wife coincided so closely. His commendation of Harriet, his admission in her favour, was especially welcome. The Eltons' insolence, which had briefly threatened to spoil the remainder of her evening, had supplied some of its finest pleasures; and she anticipated one further happy consequence—the end of Harriet's infatuation. Harriet's remarks on the incident before they left the ballroom had encouraged strong hopes. Her eyes seemed suddenly to have opened, allowing her to recognize that Mr. Elton was not the extraordinary being she had imagined. The fever had subsided, and Emma could scarcely fear that any harmful civility would set her pulse racing anew. She trusted the Eltons' ill will to provide whatever further correction through deliberate neglect might be necessary. Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not excessively in love, and Mr. Knightley disinclined to quarrel with her—what a delightful summer lay ahead!

She would not see Frank Churchill that morning. He had explained that he must forgo the pleasure of calling at Hartfield, since he was required at home by midday. She felt no regret.

Having settled these matters, considered them thoroughly, and arranged everything to her satisfaction, she was turning towards the house, her spirits refreshed for the claims of both the little boys and their grandpapa, when the great iron carriage gate swung open. Through it came two people whom she could hardly have expected less to see together: Frank Churchill, with Harriet upon his arm—Harriet herself! An instant convinced Emma that some extraordinary event had taken place. Harriet was pale and terrified, while he was endeavouring to reassure her. The iron gates stood less than twenty yards from the front door; all three were soon inside the hall, where Harriet immediately dropped into a chair and fainted.

A fainting young lady must be revived, questions answered, and surprises accounted for. Such occurrences are highly interesting, but their suspense cannot continue for long. Within a few minutes Emma knew the whole story.

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard's who had likewise attended the ball, had gone walking together along the Richmond road. Although it appeared sufficiently public to be safe, it had brought them into fright. About half a mile past Highbury, the road bent sharply and, heavily shaded on either side by elms, became secluded for a considerable distance. The young ladies had proceeded some way along this stretch when they suddenly noticed, a little ahead upon a wider piece of roadside grass, a company of gipsies.

"And remember, ma'am," Oliver said, while tears rose in his eyes in spite of his struggle to restrain them. "Oh, remember how good and young she is, and the joy and comfort she brings to everyone near her. I am sure—certain—perfectly certain—that for your sake, being so good yourself, and for her own, and for all those she makes happy, she cannot die. Heaven would never allow her to die so young."

"Hush," said Mrs. Maylie, putting her hand upon his head. "You reason like a child, poor boy. Yet you remind me of my duty all the same. For a moment I had forgotten it, Oliver; but I trust I may be forgiven. I am old, and have witnessed illness and death often enough to understand the agony of parting from those we love. I have also seen enough to know that the youngest and best are not invariably left to those who cherish them. Still, this ought to console us in our grief, for Heaven is just. Such events teach us with terrible force that a brighter world exists beyond this one, and that the journey there is swift. God's will be fulfilled! I love her, and He knows with what devotion!"

Oliver marvelled to see Mrs. Maylie's lamentations cease as she spoke, seemingly through a single act of will. Drawing herself erect, she grew calm and resolute. More astonishing still was the endurance of that resolution. Throughout the nursing and vigils that followed, she remained alert and composed, steadily discharging every responsibility that had fallen to her, and even appearing cheerful. But Oliver was young, and ignorant of the capacities of a strong mind under severe trial. How could he know them, when those who possess such minds so seldom know them themselves?

A night of anxiety followed. By morning Mrs. Maylie's fears had been only too fully confirmed: Rose was entering the early stages of a severe and dangerous fever.

"We must act, Oliver, rather than surrender to unavailing sorrow," Mrs. Maylie said, setting a finger against her lips as she looked firmly into his face. "This letter must be conveyed to Mr. Losberne with the greatest possible speed. Take it to the market town, which is no more than four miles distant by the field footpath. From there it must go by a mounted express directly to Chertsey. The people at the inn will arrange it, and I know I may rely upon you to see that it is done."

Oliver found no answer, but his expression showed his eagerness to set off immediately.
